sections.title: Detailed Brief Overview
rows: **William Wordsworth** (7 April 1770 – 23 April 1850) – Premier English **Romantic Poet** and **Nature Poet**.
Collaborated with **S.T. Coleridge** to publish **Lyrical Ballads** in **1798**, marking the official birth of English Romanticism.
Appointed **Poet Laureate** of the United Kingdom from **1843** until his death in **1850**.
Poetry is the **'spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquility'**.
Belief in **Pantheism** – God is present in every object of **Nature**; Nature as a moral teacher and healer.
**The Prelude**, or, **Growth of a Poet's Mind** (published posthumously in **1850** by his wife Mary Hutchinson).
High-scoring author section focusing on **Lyrical Ballads**, famous lines, publication dates, and definitions of poetry.

items.title: 1. Biographical Context & The Romantic Revolution
items.content:
• Born in **Cockermouth, Cumberland**, in the **Lake District**.
• Attended **St John's College, Cambridge**.
• Traveled to France during the **French Revolution** (1791–1792), where he fell in love with **Annette Vallon** (fathered a daughter, Caroline).
• Formed a lifelong literary and personal bond with his sister **Dorothy Wordsworth**, whose journals heavily inspired his poetry.
• Met **S.T. Coleridge** in 1795; their intellectual synergy produced **Lyrical Ballads** (**1798**).
• **Mnemonic for Key Associates:** **'W-C-D'** (**W**ordsworth, **C**oleridge, **D**orothy).

items.title: 2. Theory of Poetry & Poetic Diction
items.content:
• Outlined in the **Preface to Lyrical Ballads** (added in the **1800** second edition).
• Rejected the artificial, ornate **Neo-classical diction** of the 18th century (Pope, Dryden).
• Advocated for the **'real language of men'** actually spoken by common people, especially rustics and country folk.
• Defined poetry not as an intellectual exercise, but as the **'spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings'**.
• Established the famous four-stage creative process: **Observation $\rightarrow$ Emotion $\rightarrow$ Recollection in Tranquility $\rightarrow$ Composition**.

items.title: 3. Major Themes in Wordsworth's Poetry
items.content:
• **Nature and Pantheism:** Nature as a living, divine entity capable of spiritual communion (seen in *Tintern Abbey*).
• **Childhood and Memory:** The child as closer to heaven and divine truth—**'The Child is father of the Man'** (*My Heart Leaps Up*).
• **Melancholy and Solitude:** Focus on solitary figures like leech-gatherers, vagrants, and solitary reapers.
• **Memory and Time:** The power of memory to sustain the human soul against harsh realities.
• **Democratization of Subject Matter:** Elevation of humble, rural, and marginalized lives to high literary status.

items.title: 4. Analysis of Key Works: Lyrical Ballads (1798)
items.content:
• Marked the official shift from **Age of Sensibility / Enlightenment** to **Romanticism**.
• Contains 23 poems: 19 by Wordsworth and 4 by Coleridge (including **The Rime of the Ancient Mariner**).
• Wordsworth's major contributions include **Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey**, **We Are Seven**, and **Expostulation and Reply**.
• Aimed to make incidents of common life interesting by casting over them a certain coloring of imagination.

items.title: 5. Analysis of Key Works: The Prelude & Nature Odes
items.content:
• **The Prelude:** A massive autobiographical epic in blank verse addressed to Coleridge, tracing his mental and spiritual growth.
• **Ode: Intimations of Immortality:** Explores the loss of visionary gleam and childhood innocence, proposing pre-existence of the soul.
• **Lines Written in Early Spring:** Laments what man has made of man in contrast to nature's holy plan.
• **Mnemonic for Major Odes:** **'P-I-T'** (**P**relude, **I**ntimations Ode, **T**intern Abbey).

sections.title: Important Characters and Figures in Works
rows: Sister, muse, and observer whose journals inspired his imagery
Old, resilient man who teaches endurance and fortitude
Unseen highland girl singing a melancholy reaping song
Hardworking old shepherd facing financial ruin and loss of his son
Michael's son who goes to the city and falls into dissolute habits
Disabled boy whose mother (Betty Foy) searches for him
A hardened potter whose heart is softened by a loyal donkey
An old, infirm huntsman symbolizing aging and decay

sections.title: Famous Quotations and Source Works
rows: 'The sounding cataract / Haunted me like a passion'
Describes his youthful, passionate love of nature.
'A violet by a mossy stone / Half hidden from the eye!'
Lucy Gray / A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal (Lucy Poems)
Describes the rustic, hidden beauty of Lucy.
'Ten thousand saw I at a glance, / Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.'
I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud (Daffodils)
'To me the meanest flower that blows can give / Thoughts that do often lie too deep for tears.'
'The world is too much with us; late and soon, / Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers.'
The World Is Too Much With Us (1807)

items.definition: Remember **'1798'** using the rhyme: **'Seventeen ninety-eight, Romanticism opened the gate!'** This marks the exact publication year of Lyrical Ballads.
Remember his key identifiers: **P**oet Laureate (1843), **P**antheist philosopher, **N**ature poet. Acronym: **P-P-N**.

items.term: Trick 3: The Four Stages of Poetry Creation
items.definition: Use the sequence **O-E-R-C**: **O**bservation, **E**motion, **R**ecollection in tranquility, **C**omposition. Trick phrase: **'Only Elephants Rarely Cry'**.

Remember the 5 Lucy poems via the phrase **'Strange She Slept Three Times'**: **S**trange fits of passion have I known, **S**he dwelt among the untrodden ways, **I** travelled among unknown men, **S**lumber did my spirit seal, **T**hree years she grew.

Wordsworth succeeded **Robert Southey** in **1843** and was succeeded by **Alfred Lord Tennyson** in **1850**. Remember sequence: **Southey $\rightarrow$ Wordsworth $\rightarrow$ Tennyson** (**S-W-T**).

items.term: Trick 6: Major Lakes associated with Lake Poets
items.definition: Wordsworth, Coleridge, and Southey lived in the **Cumberland / Lake District**. Remember **'W-C-S in the Lake'** (**W**ordsworth, **C**oleridge, **S**outhey).

items.term: Mistake 1: Confusing Lyrical Ballads Publication Date
items.definition: Do not confuse **1798** (first edition anonymously published) with **1800** (second edition with the famous **Preface** and Wordsworth's name added).

items.term: Mistake 2: Assuming Wordsworth wrote all of Lyrical Ballads
items.definition: Students often think Wordsworth wrote the entire book. Remember that **S.T. Coleridge** contributed 4 poems, most notably **The Rime of the Ancient Mariner**.

items.term: Mistake 3: Misattributing 'Child is father of the Man'
items.definition: Many candidates confuse it with an ode or *Tintern Abbey*. It is actually from the short poem **My Heart Leaps Up** (also known as *The Rainbow*).
The poem was completed in **1805**, but published posthumously in **1850**. Always select **1850** for its official publication year.

items.term: Mistake 5: Misidentifying Wordsworth's Poetic Diction Theory
items.definition: Wordsworth advocated for the **'real language of men'** in rural life, NOT ornate classical language or difficult archaic jargon.

items.term: Mistake 6: Confusing Wordsworth with Classical / Augustan Poets
items.definition: Wordsworth broke away from **Alexander Pope** and **John Dryden**. He championed individual emotion, rustic subjects, and blank verse/ballad meters over heroic couplets.
William Wordsworth is universally known as the ultimate **Nature Poet** and a founding pillar of English **Romanticism**.
**Lyrical Ballads** (**1798**), co-authored with **S.T. Coleridge**, revolutionized English poetry by shifting focus to common life and natural language.
The **Preface to Lyrical Ballads** (**1800**) serves as the theoretical manifesto of Romantic poetry, defining poetry as **'emotion recollected in tranquility'**.
Embraced **Pantheism**, viewing nature as a living divine teacher, moral guide, and spiritual healer.
**The Prelude** (**1850**) is a landmark psychological and spiritual autobiography detailing the growth of a poet's mind.
A famous series of five short lyric poems dedicated to an enigmatic, idealized rustic girl named **Lucy**.
**Ode: Intimations of Immortality** explores the philosophical loss of childhood visionary gleam and spiritual pre-existence.
Elevated humble rural figures—leech-gatherers, shepherds (*Michael*), and solitary reapers—into subjects of high tragedy and dignity.
**'Child is father of the Man'** from *My Heart Leaps Up* emphasizes how childhood shapes adult identity.
Served as the **Poet Laureate** of the United Kingdom from **1843** until his death in **1850**.

upscNotes.content: For the UP Assistant Teacher exam, memorize the exact publication years of Lyrical Ballads (1798) and its Preface (1800), as questions frequently test these dates.
Pay close attention to Wordsworth's definition of poetry ('spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings') and be ready to match quotes to their respective poems like *Tintern Abbey* and *Daffodils*.
Do not confuse the completion date of *The Prelude* (1805) with its actual publication date (1850). Examiners use 1805 as a distractor for publication year.
Avoid assuming Coleridge wrote an equal number of poems in *Lyrical Ballads*. Coleridge contributed only 4 poems out of 23, with Wordsworth writing the rest.
Remember Dorothy Wordsworth's journals as the primary sensory and observational source for many of William's most famous descriptions, including *Daffodils*.

keyTakeaways: William Wordsworth is the chief **Nature Poet** and pioneer of **Romanticism** in English literature.
**Lyrical Ballads** (**1798**), co-written with **Coleridge**, marked the birth of the Romantic movement.
His poetic creed emphasizes the **'real language of men'** and **'emotion recollected in tranquility'**.
**The Prelude** (**1850**) is his monumental autobiographical epic tracing spiritual and mental development.
Key philosophical themes include **Pantheism**, childhood innocence (*Child is father of the Man*), and rustic simplicity.
He served as **Poet Laureate** from **1843** until **1850**.
Famous works include *Tintern Abbey*, *Daffodils*, *The Solitary Reaper*, and *Michael*.
